title:
Comment of Anne Lebo in Docket(s)/Project(s) P-15423-000
Submission Date: 9/26/2026

documents.name: 151387.txt
documents.text:
Anne Lebo, Camp Hill, PA.
To the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission:

Re: FERC Project No. P-15423-000, DeepGreen Cook Inlet Subsea-Compute & Infrastructure Hub Project

I am writing to express my strong opposition to advancing the proposed DeepGreen subsea data center project in Cook Inlet.

I love Alaska. I love its wild places, its wildlife, its rivers, its salmon and the extraordinary ecosystems that still exist there. I am not opposed to technology, renewable energy or innovation. But innovation should never mean gambling with an ecosystem that cannot be replaced.

Cook Inlet is not an empty piece of ocean.

The proposed project would involve approximately 330 to 350 tidal turbines, 66 subsea data center pods, approximately 1,650 acres of seabed and a roughly 3.5 mile armored subsea power and fiber optic cable. The proposed system is expected to generate approximately 100 megawatts, primarily to power the underwater data center.

That is an enormous industrial footprint in an environment that already supports endangered wildlife, salmon and important fisheries.

I keep asking myself one simple question: Why Cook Inlet?

Why should one of Alaska’s most important marine ecosystems become the testing ground for this kind of industrial AI infrastructure?

Cook Inlet is alive. It is salmon, beluga whales, fish, birds, marine mammals, tidal flats and an incredibly complex food web. The fact that this infrastructure would be underwater does not make its environmental footprint disappear. It simply puts that footprint beneath the surface, where many of the consequences may be much harder to see.

The Cook Inlet beluga population is federally endangered. NOAA Fisheries identifies habitat alteration, underwater noise, vessel traffic and prey limitations among the threats facing these whales. NOAA also explains that belugas rely heavily on sound for communication, navigation, finding prey and other essential behaviors.

This project would introduce hundreds of underwater turbines, construction activity, maintenance activity, vessel traffic and additional sources of underwater sound into that environment.

That deserves extraordinary scrutiny.

What will hundreds of turbines operating together sound like?

What will construction and installation sound like?

Could noise interfere with beluga communication or echolocation?

Could repeated disturbance cause belugas to avoid important feeding or other habitat?

How will the project affect an endangered population that is already under pressure from human activity?

These questions must be answered with rigorous, site specific science before this project advances.

And then there are the salmon.

ADF&G confirms that all five species of Pacific salmon are commercially harvested in Upper Cook Inlet. Salmon are not simply another species in this ecosystem. They connect Alaska’s rivers, streams, estuaries and marine waters. They support wildlife, commercial fisheries, subsistence, recreation, communities and Alaska’s economy.

No salmon, no healthy lands.

That connection is exactly why I am so concerned about putting an enormous industrial installation on the floor of Cook Inlet.

I want to know precisely how this project could affect salmon migration, feeding, spawning and rearing habitat. I want to know what will happen to sediment, turbidity, currents, benthic organisms and the prey species that salmon depend upon.

What happens during construction?

What happens during maintenance?

What happens when equipment fails?

What happens if a turbine is damaged?

What happens if a cable breaks?

What happens during an earthquake?

What happens when extreme currents, sediment or ice interact with this infrastructure?

And most importantly, what happens if we are wrong?

The fact that tidal energy is renewable does not mean it is impact free. Renewable energy is important, but every form of energy infrastructure has an environmental footprint. Calling something renewable cannot substitute for actually determining what it will do to the ecosystem where it is placed.

The same is true of the data center itself.

The purpose of the turbines is to power an underwater computing facility. That means this is not simply a renewable energy project. It is a major industrial computing operation being placed on the seabed.

Before anything moves forward, the public deserves clear answers about what happens when a subsea computing pod fails, becomes obsolete or needs to be replaced.

Who retrieves it?

Who pays for the retrieval?

What happens to the materials inside it?

What happens to damaged cables and turbines?

Who is responsible for complete removal if the project is abandoned?

What financial guarantees will ensure that Alaska taxpayers are not eventually left with an underwater industrial cleanup project?

Those guarantees should be established before this project advances.

I am also deeply concerned about cumulative impacts.

Cook Inlet already experiences substantial human activity. NOAA has identified vessel traffic, industrial development, dredging, pile driving and other sources of human generated noise as concerns for Cook Inlet belugas.

We should not look at this project in isolation and ask only whether it causes measurable harm by itself. We need to ask what additional pressure it places on an ecosystem that is already experiencing multiple pressures.

There also needs to be a serious alternatives analysis.

If the purpose is to provide computing capacity using renewable energy, why must the computing facility itself be placed on the seabed?

Why can’t the data center be located on land?

Why can’t renewable generation and computing infrastructure be separated?

What terrestrial alternatives were considered?

What other locations were considered?

What environmental impacts would be avoided by choosing another location?

The fact that engineers can build something does not automatically mean that it belongs in a particular environment.

Alaska should absolutely pursue innovation and renewable energy. But Alaska can do that while protecting the resources that make it extraordinary.

We have other places where data centers can be built.

We have other places where technology can be tested.

We do not have another Cook Inlet.

We do not have another population of Cook Inlet belugas.

We cannot simply manufacture another wild salmon ecosystem if we damage the one we have.

The current FERC proceeding concerns a preliminary permit and does not itself authorize construction. That makes this stage especially important. This is the time to demand the scientific information necessary to determine whether this project is appropriate before the process moves any further.

I ask FERC to require comprehensive, independent analysis of the project’s potential impacts on Cook Inlet belugas, salmon, fisheries, benthic habitat, sediment and water quality, underwater noise, thermal effects, electromagnetic effects, tidal currents, vessel traffic, seismic hazards, ice, cable and turbine failures, emergency response and cumulative impacts.

I also ask that alternatives to placing the data center and associated infrastructure in Cook Inlet be seriously evaluated.

Please do not allow the word “innovative” to become a substitute for environmental evidence.

Cook Inlet has existed long before AI, data centers and any of the companies proposing to use its waters. It deserves to remain healthy long after all of us are gone.

There are some places where the smartest thing we can build is a boundary.

Cook Inlet should be one of them.

Please protect the belugas.

Please protect the salmon.

Please protect the fisheries.

Please protect the wildness that makes Alaska irreplaceable.

And please do not make an endangered ecosystem the proving ground for an experimental underwater industrial complex.

Sincerely,

Anne Lebo
Concerned Citizen, Wildlife Activist & Conservationist
